svg.text: HYDROSTATIC WEIGHING — you never weigh the object in water, you weigh the WATER

The buoyant force on a submerged object has an equal and opposite reaction on the liquid, so the scale under the dish reads it directly. No below-balance hook and no special balance. Two ways to hold the load; the method below is the same for both.
A — ON A THREAD
0.3 mm fishing line, laced straight through the washer bores
B — ON THE BELL’S OWN ROD
rigid, cannot swing, and the pan is already on it
THE CALLOUTS, SAME ON BOTH
The stand rests on the BENCH — never on the scale, the dish, or the bench surface the scale sits on. If it touches, you are weighing the stand.
A mark at the waterline — scribed on the rod, taped on the line. The blank reading uses the SAME mark.
The stack FULLY under, touching nothing: not the bottom, not the walls, not the rim.
The PLA pan goes in too. Measure it rather than assuming it — note 7.
A SHALLOW dish, not a tall beaker: less thread or rod under water, so the blank stays a small correction, and less chance of fouling a wall.
Tared to zero BEFORE anything goes in, so the reading is displacement and nothing else.
THE METHOD
Weigh the load dry — washers, pan, nut: everything that hangs permanently submerged. That is m_dry.

text.tspan: Dish of water on the scale. TARE to zero.

svg.text: BLANK: lower the bare thread (or the bare rod) to the mark. Read B.
Re-tare, fit the load, lower to the SAME mark. Read L.
m_disp = L − B, and m_app = m_dry − m_disp.
Take the blank only if the scale can see it
Thread, 0.3 mm line: B ≈ 0.014 g = 0.008 Pa. Rod, Ø3: B ≈ 0.10 g
= 0.06 Pa. On a 1 g scale both are invisible — skip it. Take it
only at 0.1 g or finer, where it also cancels a hook, a bag or a
soaked knot. At 1 g a CARRIER still matters, though: a wire hook or
a mesh bag displaces grams. Lace the washers onto the line.
WHICH ONE
Thread if you want the smallest correction: a thin line is nearly
invisible to the scale, and the washers lace onto it through their own
Ø13 bores, so there is no carrier to account for.
Rod if you want the load to sit still. It cannot swing into a wall,
the pan is already fitted, and the depth mark is easy to hit twice.
Its larger blank is exactly cancelled, so the choice is ergonomics.
WHAT TO WATCH
The stand must be mechanically separate from the scale. This is the one mistake that ruins the reading without looking wrong.
Contact with the dish transfers weight — bottom, walls and rim all count. A thread lets the load swing, so let it settle and watch the load, not the display.
Lace the washers on the line itself; do not use a hook or a mesh bag. A carrier is a second material with its own displacement, and you would
end up measuring the ratio of washers-plus-carrier, which is not a thing you need. If you must use one, blank it with the carrier fitted and empty.
THE SCALE IS THE REFERENCE, AND ITS SPAN MATTERS MORE THAN ITS RESOLUTION. P scales with the scale’s gain, so an unchecked span goes
straight through: 0.57 % of reading at 500 Pa unchecked, against 0.26 % checked to ±0.1 %, and 0.20 % on a 0.1 g scale. Buy one calibration
weight, not a better scale, and check it near the working mass. Even unchecked, this is 5× better than the part’s own 3 % span spec.
Leave no VISIBLE bubble. At 1 g resolution twenty 3 mm bubbles come to 0.17 Pa and are invisible, but a single 1 cm³ one is a whole division.
Re-tare between the blank and the load: water evaporates and scales drift.
PRINT THE PAN SOLID. A 1 cm³ internal void is 1 g of buoyancy = 0.57 Pa, and a void that slowly floods moves the tare with nothing to show it.
On a 1 g scale, DO NOT weigh the pan’s displacement: 16 g read to ±1 g is ±0.57 Pa and it is a CONSTANT offset. Compute it as m_dry/1.24
instead — PLA density is good to ~3 %, so ±0.27 Pa, twice as good. And weigh 24 washers rather than 12 for the ratio: it halves that term.
Record the water temperature: it moves m_disp by 0.04 % over 10–30 °C, which is negligible, but §2.2 asks for it anyway.
